Learn them exactly and hold them even when the child protests and even when a parent, in a soft moment, waives them, because the routine is the parents' instrument and inconsistency from staff undermines it. Never override a parent's instruction about their own small child on your own judgement, and never make yourself the fun adult who bends the rules the parents enforce; that is a cheap affection and it costs you the parents' trust.

**Teenagers.** The hardest age, and the one where boundaries are tested daily. A teenager in a wealthy house often has money, freedom and a sense of entitlement that outruns their judgement, and they will, sooner or later, ask you to do something their parents would not sanction: cover an absence, buy something forbidden, drive them somewhere unapproved, keep a secret. You must be warm, respectful and genuinely on their side as a person, and you must not become their accomplice against their parents. The line is precise. You may keep a teenager's ordinary confidences, the small dignities of a young person's private life, and you must, or they will never trust you. You may not conceal from parents anything that touches the child's safety: substances, an older stranger, a real risk, a plan that could end badly. Decide where that line sits before you are asked to cross it at eleven at night, because you will be asked, and the amateur decides in the moment and decides wrong.

**Adult children.** A different problem entirely. The principal's grown son or daughter may have their own standing in the family, their own money, and their own expectations of the staff, and they may issue you instructions as though the house were theirs. Sometimes it partly is. But adult children are not usually your employer, and an instruction from one that contradicts the principal's standing arrangement is a trap, not a command. Serve them with courtesy and real willingness; route anything that commits the family's money, alters a standing arrangement, or sets one generation against another quietly back through the office or the principal. The adult child who is testing whether you will help them go around their parent is reading your answer closely, and the right answer is gracious help within your remit and calm deferral beyond it.

Across every age, one rule governs: the parents own the parenting, and you protect the child within the frame the parents set. You are neither the disciplinarian nor the indulgent friend. You are the reliable adult who keeps the child safe and the routine intact and repeats nothing about the child that the child, or the parents, would not wish repeated.

**12.4 · The elder generation, and undeclared authority**

Many households contain a generation above the principal: a parent or parents of the principal or the spouse, sometimes resident, sometimes visiting, sometimes governing from a distance. Their authority is almost never written down and almost always real. A grandmother who founded the fortune, a father who handed the business to his son, a matriarch whose approval still settles family questions, carries a weight that no organisational chart records and that a newcomer routinely underestimates.

Read this weight early, because you will meet it as a surprise otherwise. The principal, who commands everyone else without hesitation, may defer to their own mother in a way that reorders the whole house when she is present. Standing arrangements bend around her visit.

Menus change, schedules soften, the register of the house grows more formal or more careful. If you treat the elder as merely another guest, you will misjudge a dozen small things and be quietly marked as someone who cannot read a family.

The practical needs of the elder generation are also distinct, and increasingly so as the profession serves families living longer. Elderly members may have medical routines, mobility requirements, dietary restrictions, medication schedules, carers or nurses who must be coordinated with the household, and a pace that the rest of the fast-moving family does not keep.

Serving them well means slowing down, offering more time and more patience than the principal's own tempo trains into you, and treating dignity as the first requirement. An older person who has been powerful all their life feels the loss of independence acutely; the professional supplies help in a way that never announces itself as help, that lets the elder keep the appearance and the feeling of managing their own life.

There is a specific confidentiality that surrounds the elder generation's health and decline, and it runs inward as much as outward. A family may be managing an ageing parent's failing memory, a diagnosis not yet shared, a mobility that is worsening, and they may not all be equally informed or equally ready to speak of it.

You may know more than some family members do about how a grandmother is truly faring, because you are present daily and they are not. That knowledge is held, not distributed. You do not become the person who tells the daughter what the son has not, however kindly the impulse.

**12.5 · The extended family and the inner circle**

Beyond the household proper stands a wider ring: siblings of the principal, cousins, in-laws, the principal's oldest friends, godchildren, and the long-serving assistants and advisers who have the family's confidence. These people are not your employer and not, strictly, your responsibility, and yet they carry expectations of the staff, arrive with needs, and can shape your standing through nothing more than a word to the principal.

The difficulty is that their authority is ambiguous by design. The principal's brother who treats the house as his own may genuinely have the run of it, or may be presuming on a welcome that has limits, and you often cannot tell which. The safe posture is generous courtesy without commitment: you extend to the extended family the warmth and competence of the house, and you commit nothing that belongs to the principal, no money, no standing arrangement, no confidential information, without checking.

When the principal's cousin asks you to book the family's usual villa for her own holiday, or to put a purchase on the household account, you do not refuse and you do not simply comply; you help graciously and confirm quietly with the office, framing it never as suspicion of the cousin but as the ordinary way the house handles arrangements.

The inner circle of trusted assistants and advisers deserves particular care, and it connects to the material on the office and the other staff covered elsewhere; here the point is narrower. The principal's oldest personal assistant, the family's longtime lawyer, the friend who is consulted on everything, these people have a line to the principal that you do not, and a memory of the family that predates you by decades.

Treat them as senior colleagues to be cultivated, never as rivals to be outmanoeuvred. A great deal of what you need to know, the family's real preferences, the history behind a rule, the reason a certain name is never mentioned, lives in these people, and it is given to the professional who is respectful and withheld from the one who is territorial.

**12.6 · House guests, and serving without a brief**

Guests are a distinct discipline because they arrive without the years of accumulated knowledge that let you serve the family. You know the principal's coffee, the spouse's chair, the children's routine. You know nothing about the couple arriving on Friday for the weekend, and yet the family's standing among their own friends depends partly on how those guests are looked after. You are, for three days, extending the family's reputation to people you have never met.

The work begins before they arrive, and quietly. Learn what can be learned in advance without intrusion: the guests' names and how they are addressed, any dietary needs or allergies, whether they travel with their own staff, roughly what the visit is for, a birthday, a business friendship, a family obligation, because the purpose sets the register.

A close old friend of the principal is served with warmth and informality; a business guest the principal wishes to impress is served with visible polish; a difficult relative who must be endured is served with faultless, unreadable courtesy. Ask the principal or the spouse, once and efficiently, for anything you cannot infer, rather than guessing at the things that matter.

Then, on arrival, you read the guest quickly and directly, because you have no history to draw on. Watch how they respond to the house. Some guests are made comfortable by attentive, formal service; others are made deeply uneasy by it and want to feel they are in a home, not a hotel, and pressing service on such a person reads as suffocation.

Offer, observe the response, and calibrate. A guest who waves away the offer of unpacking wants space; a guest who seems lost in the house wants guidance. The whole art is to make a stranger feel known within an hour, which you do not by grand gestures but by small anticipations: the phone charger already by the bed, the note explaining how the house works, the quiet solving of the thing they were about to ask for.

Two boundaries govern guest service and both matter. First, a guest is not your principal, and their instructions do not override the family's standing arrangements or their household's rules; you serve the guest generously within the frame the family sets, and you do not, for instance, breach a house security protocol because a guest finds it inconvenient.

Second, and more delicate, what you observe of guests is held as closely as what you observe of the family. Guests reveal themselves in a private house, and the family's friendships are not yours to comment on, to the family or to anyone. You saw nothing, you heard nothing, the weekend simply went well.

**12.7 · Personalities and rivalries, and the discipline of neutrality**

Every family has its currents: the sibling who resents the favoured one, the marriage under strain, the adult child at odds with a parent, the old alliance and the old wound. A family with a great deal of money has all of this and more, because money adds stakes to every ordinary human friction, and inheritance, succession and control turn private feeling into open contest.

You will be living inside these currents, and you will be pulled toward them, because human beings under strain seek allies, and you are conveniently present, discreet, and dependent on their goodwill.

The discipline is neutrality, and it is more demanding than it sounds. Neutrality is not blandness and not the absence of warmth; you can be genuinely fond of everyone and still take no side. It is the steady refusal to become anyone's instrument, informant or ally against another member of the family.

When the principal's sister confides her frustration with the principal and looks to you for agreement, you offer sympathy for the feeling and no verdict on the person: you are sorry it is difficult, you understand it is hard, and you say nothing that could be repeated as your opinion of the principal. When one spouse fishes for what the other has been doing, you know nothing useful, warmly and without the coldness that itself gives things away.

The particular trap is the invitation to take a side dressed as ordinary conversation. A family member, especially one who feels aggrieved, will offer you their reading of a rivalry and wait to see whether you join them. To join, even by a sympathetic murmur about the other person, is to be recruited, and recruitment is fatal, because the family's alliances shift and the person you sided with today may be reconciled with your target tomorrow, leaving you exposed as the staff member who spoke against a member of the family.

Every family member must believe, correctly, that you are fond of them and fair to all of them and would never carry a word about them to anyone. That belief is worth more than any single alliance could ever be, and it survives only if it is true.

Hold, too, a practical neutrality in the small mechanics of favour. Do not visibly do more for the family member you like best. Do not let the children see that one of them is easier to serve.

Do not let the extended family sense a hierarchy of your warmth. The appearance of even-handedness is part of the substance of it, and in a family alert to slight, an unevenness you did not intend is read as a judgement you did not make.

**12.8 · Whose instruction wins**

Sooner or later two members of the family will instruct you in ways that cannot both be honoured. The spouse says one thing and the principal another. The adult son commits you to a plan the father has not sanctioned.

The grandmother, visiting, quietly countermands the routine the parents have set for the children. This is not a rare crisis; it is a regular feature of serving a system rather than a person, and the professional needs a settled way to handle it that does not require heroics in the moment.

Begin from the structure you established on arrival. In a well-read household you already know, roughly, whose authority governs which domain: that the spouse owns the domestic register, that the office owns spending above a threshold, that the parents own the children's routine, that the principal owns the things the principal reserves.

Most apparent contradictions are not real contradictions but boundary questions, and knowing the boundaries answers them: the grandmother does not, in fact, get to rewrite the children's bedtime, and you hold the parents' rule with warmth and without confrontation, "I'll check with their mother, she likes to keep them to the usual on school nights," which defers to the parents' authority while giving the grandmother no cause for offence.

Where the contradiction is real and inside one domain, two people with genuine claim instructing you oppositely, the rule is simple to state and hard to practise: you do not adjudicate, and you do not quietly obey the last or the loudest voice. You surface the conflict upward or sideways to the person or structure that can resolve it, and you do it without drama and without casting either party as the problem.

"I've had slightly different steers on this from both of you and I want to get it right, so let me confirm the plan with the office and come back to you both" is a sentence that offends no one and protects you completely. The instinct to just quietly do what the more frightening person said is the instinct that gets you blamed by the other, because in a family the losing party finds out, and finds out that you chose.

Never, in resolving a contradiction, make yourself the messenger of one family member's displeasure to another. If the principal has overruled the spouse's instruction, the principal tells the spouse, or the office does; you do not carry "he said no" between a married couple. You execute the resolution once it exists and you stay out of the delivery of the bad news, because the staff member who becomes the conduit for a family's internal conflict is the staff member the family eventually resents for knowing too much of it.

**12.9 · Confidentiality inside the family**

You will already understand confidentiality outward: nothing about the family leaves the house. The harder and less obvious discipline is confidentiality inward, between members of the same family, and it is where good people fail through kindness rather than malice.

You are present across the whole family in a way no single member is. You move between the principal's world and the spouse's, between the parents and the children, between the household and the extended family, and you accumulate, without seeking it, a knowledge of each that the others do not have.

You know the spouse's plan before the principal does. You know what the teenager is worried about. You know the elder parent's diagnosis, or the sum a cousin borrowed, or the reason two siblings are not speaking.

This knowledge is not yours to move around the family, and the temptation to move it is constant, because sharing it feels helpful, or intimate, or like the natural thing a trusted person would do.

Hold the line absolutely: what you learn of one family member you do not repeat to another, even when they are married, even when they are parent and child, even when the person asking clearly loves the person you would be discussing. The spouse asking what the principal has planned, the mother asking what the teenager confided, the sister asking what the brother said about the inheritance, all meet the same warm, immovable non-answer.

You are not a channel through which the family learns about itself. If a family member wants to know something about another, the professional's reflex is to hand the question back to the person who owns the answer: "you'd want to ask him that yourself, I think," offered gently, closes the door without slamming it.

This inward discretion is what finally makes you safe to have in the house. A family that senses you carry information between its members will, correctly, begin to guard themselves in front of you, and a guarded family cannot be served well, because service depends on the family being at ease in your presence.

The staff member who never repeats anything, in either direction, becomes over time invisible in the best sense: a person before whom the family can simply be itself, because they have learned that nothing said in front of you travels anywhere at all.

**12.10 · Pets, and the staff they keep**

Do not underestimate the animals. In many houses the pets occupy a place in the family's affection that outranks a good deal of the human hierarchy, and their care is treated with a seriousness that surprises the newcomer. A principal who is composed about a cancelled flight may be genuinely distressed by a limping dog, and the professional who dismisses the animals as a minor duty misreads the emotional geography of the house.

Pets in a serious household frequently come with their own logistics: a veterinarian on call, a groomer, a walker or a dedicated handler, a diet as particular as any family member's, travel arrangements that can rival a person's in complexity, because the dog flies too, and the horse, and the arrangements for them cross borders and require documents. Learn the animals' routines as you learn the children's, hold them with the same consistency, and coordinate the people who care for them as part of the household rather than as an afterthought.

The dog walker and the groom are staff of the house, and the same disciplines of scheduling, courtesy and neutrality apply to them.

There is also a small confidentiality and a small diplomacy around pets, as there is around everything in a family. The animal may be a point of tension, one spouse devoted and the other tolerant, a child promised a puppy against a parent's wishes, an elderly dog whose decline the family is not ready to face.

Handle these with the same care you bring to any family feeling. And treat the animals themselves with genuine kindness whether or not anyone is watching, because a family reads how you are with their dog as a reliable sign of who you are, and they are not wrong to.

**12.11 · Belonging to a household without becoming family**

The final discipline is the subtlest, and it holds all the others together. You will spend more time in this family's life than many of their relatives do. You will know their mornings, their habits, their children, their grief.

You will be present at holidays and crises and quiet ordinary evenings, and the family, particularly a warm one, particularly a self-made one without an inherited model of what staff are, may come to speak of you as one of the family and mean it kindly. This is the most dangerous kindness in the profession, and the emotional intelligence to hold it correctly is what separates the durable professional from the one who is eventually, painfully, let go.

You belong to the household. You do not belong to the family. The distinction is not coldness; you may love this family, and be loved by them, and the work is better for it.

The distinction is that your position rests on a role, not on kinship, and the role has a boundary that kinship does not. Family members may fail each other and be forgiven forever; you may not. Family members share in the family's fortunes; you are paid, and can be unpaid.

When you forget this, when you begin to feel entitled to a family member's consideration, to act on the assumption that your place is secure because you are loved, to take the liberties a relative takes, you begin, invisibly, to become a problem, and the warmth that felt like belonging withdraws exactly when you have come to depend on it.

Hold the warmth and the boundary at once. Accept the affection gracefully and never presume on it. Be present in the family's intimate life and never mistake presence for membership.

Let them call you one of the family and know, privately and without bitterness, that you are not, because that private clarity is what lets you keep serving them well through the seasons when the affection cools, as in any long relationship it sometimes will. The professional who needed to be family is wounded by every reminder that they are staff.

The professional who is at peace being staff, and gives the family the whole of their care without needing the family's love in return, is the one a household keeps for twenty years.

This is the emotional discipline the whole role finally asks of you. To be close without clinging, warm without presuming, essential without being owed, and to find your security not in being loved by the family, which you cannot control, but in the quality of what you do, which you can.

Belong to the house completely. Keep, always, the small clear space that is yours alone, and that no household, however dear, is ever quite allowed to enter.

**CHAPTER SUMMARY**

You are hired by one person and you serve a family, a system of people with uneven power and separate standards. The spouse often sets the domestic register you live inside, and you serve both partners while siding with neither. Children change the moral weight of the work: you protect them within the frame the parents set, keep young children's routines, keep teenagers' ordinary confidences but not their dangerous secrets, and defer adult children's overreach gracefully. The elder generation holds undeclared authority and needs patient, dignified care, and their health is held closely, inward as well as outward. The extended family and inner circle get generous courtesy without commitment. Guests are served without a brief by learning what you can in advance and reading them fast on arrival. Neutrality inside the family's rivalries is absolute: you are no one's instrument or informant. When instructions conflict, you surface the conflict rather than obey the loudest voice, and you never carry a family's bad news between its members. Confidentiality runs inward as strictly as outward, and it is what finally makes you safe to have in the house. The pets and their care are taken seriously. And the whole is held together by one discipline: belong to the household completely, and never become part of the family, finding your security in the quality of your work rather than in being loved.

## Working with the other staff

*Colleagues, hierarchy, and the quiet politics of a house*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

Map the other people who run a household and understand what each of them controls, fears, and needs from you. Locate yourself precisely in the hierarchy, and learn to manage upward toward the principal and the office, downward toward the staff you supervise, and sideways toward your peers, each of which is a different discipline. Recognise the standing politics of a house, its favourites, its gatekeepers, its long-tenured resisters, and the permanent tension between the family office and the household, and move through them without becoming a piece of them. Give instructions and corrections without humiliating anyone. Understand covering for a colleague and the exact point at which loyalty becomes complicity. And build a professional reputation that travels, because the world of private service is very small and it talks.

**13.1 · The people you actually work beside**

A great deal of your success will rest not on the family and not on the office but on the ten or fifteen other people who keep the house standing, and almost none of your training so far has been about them. The principal is one relationship.

The staff are a dozen, and each of the dozen can make your working life smooth or wretched in ways the family will never see and never adjudicate. Learn who they are, what they own, and what earns their cooperation, because you will get none of your own work done without it.

**Housekeepers.** The people who hold the physical house in their hands and, with it, most of its secrets. A senior housekeeper often knows more about the family's real life, its habits, its tensions, its illnesses, its favourite and least favourite guests, than anyone else on the payroll, because she is in every room every day and the family stops noticing her. She is proud, exacting, and frequently long-serving, and she will read any newcomer as a possible threat to a domain she has run without interference for years. Earn her by respecting the domain: never move, reorganise, or criticise her work without asking, learn her standard before you impose yours, and be seen to defend her time against unreasonable demands from above.

**Chefs.** Creative, territorial, and central to the family's daily pleasure in a way few other roles are, because people notice their food three times a day and remember a bad meal. A private chef guards the kitchen, the menus, and the supplier relationships as a professional guards a reputation, and resents being treated as a short-order cook or being blindsided by a dinner for twelve announced at four o'clock. Earn a chef with notice, with accurate numbers, with early and precise intelligence on guests, allergies, and the principal's shifting appetites, and by never, ever relaying a criticism of the food as though it were your own.

**Drivers and chauffeurs.** Often the calmest and most discreet people in the house, and among the most useful to you, because they see the principal at unguarded moments, hold the real texture of the day's movements, and hear a great deal in the quiet of a car. A good driver is a source of gold if you treat him as a colleague and a menace if you treat him as a taxi. Earn him by protecting his schedule, respecting the boundary between driving and errand-running, and never leaving him waiting outside for two hours because you failed to plan the day you asked him to execute.

**Security.** A standing function with its own director, its own discipline, and, on certain questions, an authority that simply exceeds yours. Security people are trained to be suspicious, to control information, and to say no, and a house manager who treats them as an obstacle will find every movement made harder. Earn them by feeding them accurate information early, never surprising them with a guest or a movement, and understanding that when they overrule you on a matter of safety they are doing their job and not challenging your standing.

**Nannies.** The most emotionally charged role in the house and the one most likely to generate friction with everyone, because a nanny's loyalty is to the child, and that loyalty will, correctly, override the household's convenience and sometimes the family's own stated wishes. A good nanny sits close to the parents' hearts and can be quietly powerful. Earn her by respecting the primacy of the children's routine, never using the children to move your own agenda, and treating the nursery as a domain you support rather than command.

**Gardeners and grounds staff.** Often the least visible and most stable people on an estate, working to seasons rather than to the day, proud of work that takes years to mature, and easily forgotten in the planning of everything else. Earn them with notice, with respect for the long horizon of their work, and by remembering they exist when you schedule the events that trample their lawns.

**Personal and executive assistants.** The office-side people who hold the principal's diary and correspondence and who, as you were taught earlier, sit closer to the principal's daily attention than almost anyone in the house. Much of what reaches you reaches you through them. Treat the principal's EA as a peer to be cultivated, never as a subordinate to be instructed, whatever your titles seem to say.

**The estate team.** In larger operations, a maintenance manager, an estate director, project people, and the trades who come and go. They run on budgets and timelines rather than on the day's caprice, and they resent last-minute demands that ignore both. Earn them with lead time and with a reputation for being the person who fought to get their invoices paid.

**13.2 · Where you sit**

Before you can manage anyone you must know exactly where you stand, and the peculiarity of your position, which you met earlier in a different form, is that you stand in two places at once. You sit at the bottom of the office chart and at the top of the house chart, and you are the hinge between them.

This double position is the source of most of your authority and all of its ambiguity, and until you have felt it precisely you will overreach in one direction or shrink in the other.

Read the line carefully. Above you sits the office, in the person of the chief of staff, the estate director, or, in a smaller house, the principal directly. Below you sit the residence staff whose work you coordinate.

Beside you sit your peers, other managers, the principal's EA, the head of security, people whose authority runs parallel to yours and does not answer to it. Your standing with each of these three directions is earned by an entirely different behaviour, and the commonest failure in the whole of household management is to apply the manner of one direction to another: to manage a peer as though he reported to you, or to defer to a subordinate as though he were a peer, or to treat the principal as a colleague because the intimacy of the work tempted you to forget the line.

Note one thing about your authority that newcomers consistently misjudge. It is positional, not personal, and it is delegated, not owned. When you ask the housekeeper to change a standing arrangement, you are not doing so on your own account; you are exercising an authority the family and the office have lent you, and it evaporates the moment the staff conclude you are using it for yourself rather than for the house.

The manager who says "because I say so" has told the whole staff that his authority rests on nothing but his title, which is the weakest possible foundation, and they will test it. The manager who anchors an instruction in the family's standard, "the principal likes the cars ready ten minutes early," borrows an authority that no one below him can argue with, because it does not belong to him and cannot be resented as his.

**13.3 · Managing up**

Managing upward is the discipline of being useful to the people above you without being needy, invisible about your difficulties without being dishonest, and reliably informative without ever wasting their attention. It is a real skill, and most people are poor at it, because they confuse being managed well with being liked.

The first rule of managing up is to make your manager's job easier, not harder, which means solving what you can solve and escalating only what genuinely requires them. Every problem you carry to the chief of staff that you could have solved yourself is a small withdrawal from their confidence in you; every problem you conceal that you should have raised is a larger one, deferred.

The professional judgement is knowing the difference, and the test is simple: bring them decisions that are theirs to make and outcomes they need to know, and keep from them the ordinary friction of the day that is precisely what you are paid to absorb.

The second rule is to report in the register your manager values, which you must read rather than assume. A controller wants tidy figures and no surprises. A chief of staff from a corporate background wants a short written brief and a clear recommendation.

An old-money estate director may want none of it in writing and all of it in a quiet word. Match the register, and your competence is legible; ignore it, and the same competence goes unread.

The third rule concerns the principal directly, and it is the most delicate. You will, in most houses, deal with the principal rarely and with the office constantly, and when the principal does reach you directly it is significant. Managing up toward the principal is not the same as managing up toward the office.

With the office you are a professional reporting to professionals. With the principal you are removing thought from their head, which means you do not, as a rule, bring them problems, options, or the machinery of how a thing was done. You bring them the settled outcome and the single decision only they can make.

A principal who is made to feel the workings of the house has been failed, however impressive the workings.

**A HAZARD PECULIAR TO THIS PROFESSION**

The intimacy of the work will, sooner or later, tempt you to treat the principal as a confidant, especially in a self-made house where the principal has no inherited model of staff and may, on a Monday, invite exactly that closeness. Accept the warmth and never bank on it. The line can be redrawn without warning, by the principal, in an instant, and the professional who has kept a private distance survives the redrawing while the one who forgot the line is wounded by it. Manage up with warmth, never with the assumption of friendship.

**13.4 · Managing down**

Managing the staff below you is where most household managers are tested hardest and trained least, because giving orders to grown professionals, many of them older than you and longer in the house, is genuinely difficult and no one teaches it. The whole art is to secure willing cooperation rather than grudging compliance, because a house runs on the former and grinds on the latter, and the difference is invisible in any single instruction and total across a year.

Begin from the recognition that you cannot do their jobs better than they can. You do not know the linen or the kitchen or the engine of the car as they do, and the moment you pretend to, you lose them. Your authority is not technical superiority; it is the coordination of the whole, the holding of the standard, and the relationship with the family that none of them has.

Manage from that ground, and defer visibly to their craft within their own domains, and you will find that people who are respected as experts are far more willing to be coordinated as a team.

Give instructions that are clear, that carry the reason where the reason helps, and that leave the person their dignity and their method. There is a difference between "the principal would like the terrace cleared and set for eight by six o'clock" and "go and clear the terrace," and the difference is not politeness for its own sake; it is that the first gives the person the standard and the deadline and trusts them to reach it their own way, while the second treats a skilled adult as a pair of hands. Trust people with the what and the why, and leave them the how wherever you safely can.

Be scrupulously fair in the distribution of the work no one wants, the late nights, the holiday cover, the tedious jobs, because nothing corrodes a team faster than the perception that the manager protects his favourites and dumps the misery on the rest. Keep a schedule that is written, visible, and honoured, so that duty and cover and time off are matters of record rather than of the manager's mood, and so that no one can believe they are being singled out when they are simply taking their turn.

**13.5 · How to correct without humiliating**

Correction is the specific skill that separates a manager staff will follow from one they merely tolerate, and it rests on a single principle: correct the error, protect the person. The aim is never to be proven right, to relieve your own irritation, or to establish who is in charge.

The aim is that the thing is done correctly next time and that the person is more willing, not less, to work for you afterward. Every correction that wins the point and loses the person is a defeat dressed as a victory.

Observe the rules that make this possible.

- Correct in private, always, and praise in public. A correction delivered in front of colleagues, or worse in front of the family, is remembered as a humiliation long after the substance is forgotten, and it teaches everyone watching that you are dangerous to work near.
- Correct promptly and once. Do not save up grievances for a great reckoning; address the thing when it is small, plainly, and then let it go. The manager who hoards faults and unleashes them together is feared and never trusted.
- Address the specific action, not the person's character. "The car was not fuelled and the principal was kept waiting" is a fact that can be fixed. "You are careless" is a verdict that can only be resented. One improves the work; the other makes an enemy.
- Where you can, give the correction as a standard rather than a rebuke. "We always confirm the restaurant the morning of, because tables get lost" teaches the house's way and spares the individual the sting of having been singled out.
- Listen before you conclude. The failure you are about to correct may have a cause you do not know, an instruction from above, a fault in another department, a reasonable judgement that went wrong. The manager who corrects first and learns the cause afterward is the manager who is quietly resented for being unjust.

Reserve the formal machinery, the written warning, the involvement of the office, for genuine and repeated failures, and understand that reaching for it too early spends authority you cannot easily recover. Most correction in a well-run house never becomes formal at all, because it is done early, privately, specifically, and with the person's dignity intact.

**13.6 · Managing sideways**

Your peers are the hardest relationships to manage precisely because you have no authority over them and they none over you, and yet the smooth running of the house depends on your cooperation more than on almost anything else. The head of security, the principal's EA, the chief who reports to the family rather than to you, the estate director in a parallel line, these are people you must work with daily and cannot instruct, and the whole discipline is influence without authority.

The currency of sideways relationships is reciprocity and reliability. You make the EA's life easier and she makes yours easier; you feed security accurate information early and they stop treating your requests as impositions; you give the chef the numbers he needs and he covers for you when a dinner materialises from nowhere.

None of this can be commanded, all of it can be earned, and it is earned by being, consistently, the colleague who does what he said he would do, who never lets another department take the blame for his own failure, and who shares rather than hoards.

Guard particularly against the two errors that poison peer relationships. The first is treating a peer as a subordinate, issuing to the EA or the security director the kind of instruction you would give a housemaid; nothing is resented more quickly or remembered longer. The second is competing for the family's regard, which is the deep temptation of every parallel relationship in a house, because you all serve the same principal and the principal's attention feels finite.

The manager who tries to look good by making a peer look bad has started a war he will eventually lose, because the house is small, the war is visible, and the family tires of both parties long before it takes sides.

**13.7 · The politics of a house**

Every household of any size has a politics, and it exists whether or not you choose to see it, so you had far better see it. It is not a corruption of the work; it is the human residue of a small number of people spending years in close quarters around a single source of money and attention, and it has recognisable features you can learn to read.

**The favourite.** In most houses one member of staff sits closer to the principal's affection than their title warrants, a long-serving housekeeper, a driver of twenty years, a nanny the children adore. The favourite has real informal power, can bypass the chart, and can help or hurt you out of all proportion to their rank. Do not resent the favourite and do not try to displace them; understand the relationship, respect it, and win the favourite's goodwill, because their word to the principal carries a weight yours may take years to earn.

**The gatekeeper.** Someone controls access, to the principal, to information, to the diary, to the approval you need, and it is frequently not the person the chart says it should be. It may be the EA, the chief of staff, a trusted lieutenant of no obvious rank. Identify the real gatekeepers early, because trying to reach the principal or the decision around them is the fastest way to make a permanent enemy of exactly the person whose cooperation you most need.

**The long-tenured resister.** Old houses contain people who were there long before you and expect to be there long after, and who regard every newcomer, and every change a newcomer proposes, as a judgement on the way they have always done things. You cannot overpower this person and you should not try. You win them slowly, by respecting what they built, by asking their view before you change their world, by crediting them where credit is due, and by proving over months that you are an ally of the house rather than a careerist passing through. The reforming manager who arrives and announces improvements in the first week has, in effect, declared war on the institutional memory of the house, and the institutional memory always wins.

**The office against the household.** Beneath the individuals runs a structural tension you will feel constantly: the family office wants control, documentation, budgets that hold, and risk contained, while the household wants flexibility, responsiveness, and the freedom to meet the family's actual life as it happens. These two legitimate interests pull against each other, and you, the hinge, feel the pull in your own person. The office thinks the house is extravagant and undisciplined; the house thinks the office is slow, remote, and deaf to reality. Your task is not to take a side but to be the translator both sides trust, and you earn that trust by giving the office the discipline it needs, tidy reporting, honoured budgets, no surprises, while defending the household's genuine needs to the office in the office's own language of cost, risk, and outcome.

**A RULE FOR ALL HOUSEHOLD POLITICS**

See everything and align with no faction. The moment you are perceived as belonging to a camp, the patriarch's people against the son's, the old guard against the new, the house against the office, you have converted every member of the opposing faction into an adversary and made yourself a casualty of a fight that was never yours. Your standing depends on being trusted by all sides, which is only possible if you are owned by none.

**13.8 · Gossip, and the discipline of the neutral**

The single most reliable way to destroy your standing in a house, faster than incompetence and almost as fast as a breach of confidence, is to be drawn into its gossip. Every household generates talk, about the family, about each other, about who is favoured and who is failing, and the talk is a current that will pull you in if you let it, because joining it is warm, it is bonding, and it feels like belonging.

Resist it, and understand precisely why. The colleague who gossips with you about another colleague is demonstrating, in the act, exactly what they will do to you the moment your back is turned, and you should file that demonstration rather than enjoy the confidence. The staff member who repeats to you a fault of the family is showing you the standard of discretion they hold, which is to say none, and you should be warned rather than flattered.

Every scrap of gossip you pass onward attaches your name to it and marks you, correctly, as a person who cannot be trusted with what they hear, which in this profession is the whole of the game.

This does not mean being cold, aloof, or humourless, which reads as arrogance and isolates you as surely as gossip corrupts you. It means being warm and genuinely liked while declining, gracefully and consistently, to trade in other people's reputations. You can listen without repeating.

You can be the person to whom people talk without being the person who talks, and that reputation, once established, is worth an enormous amount, because it is precisely why the difficult confidence, the one that actually matters, eventually comes to you rather than to the office gossip. Be the still point.

In the small world of a household, the person who does not carry tales becomes, over time, the only person everyone trusts.

**13.9 · Covering, and the limit of loyalty**

Staff cover for one another; it is one of the decencies of a working house, and a manager who never allowed it would be running a barracks rather than a household. When the driver is ten minutes late because his child was ill, when the housemaid missed a small thing on a hard day, when a colleague needs an hour and you can quietly absorb it, covering is the ordinary generosity that makes a team a team, and you should extend it and accept it in the small currency of daily life.

But covering has a boundary, and finding it precisely is a matter of professional survival, because the same instinct that makes you a decent colleague can make you an accomplice, and the two look identical until the moment they do not. The line runs, roughly, here: you may cover for a person, absorbing a small and honest failure to spare them an unnecessary reckoning, but you may never cover for a fact, concealing from the family or the office something they have a genuine right and need to know.

Covering the late driver is loyalty. Concealing that the driver has been drinking, or that money is missing, or that a member of staff has done something that touches the family's safety, property, or trust, is not loyalty; it is complicity, and when it surfaces, as it always eventually does, it takes you down with the person you protected.

Hold the distinction in a single test. Ask whether the thing you are being asked to hide is a private embarrassment that harms no one, or a fact that the family or the office would need in order to make a decision that is properly theirs.

The first you may, in kindness, let lie. The second you cannot conceal, because concealing it substitutes your judgement for theirs on a matter that was never yours to decide, and because your first loyalty, always, beneath every collegial decency, is to the family who employs you and not to the colleague who asks you to keep their secret.

Say so plainly when you must: that you are fond of them, that this is beyond what you can hold, and that they must put it right or you will have to. That conversation is hard, and having it honestly is precisely what marks you as someone the house can afford to trust with everything else.

**13.10 · Turf and information**

Two things function as currency inside a household, and understanding them will explain half the behaviour you would otherwise find baffling: turf, and information. People guard both, trade both, and read your handling of both as the surest sign of what kind of colleague you are.

Turf is the domain each member of staff controls, the kitchen, the nursery, the linen, the cars, the grounds, and people defend it because within it they are sovereign and competent and safe. Almost every avoidable conflict in a house is a border dispute, a manager reorganising a domain that was not his to reorganise, a colleague reaching across a line to do a favour that reads as an incursion.

Respect turf scrupulously. Ask before you enter another person's domain, credit them within it, and never be seen to command inside a territory whose expert is standing right there. You lose nothing by deferring inside another's turf, and you gain the one thing that makes the house work, which is their willingness to let you coordinate across all of it.

Information is the other currency, and it is more dangerous, because it accumulates to you naturally, as the hinge, and the temptation to spend it for advantage is constant. You will know things others do not, movements, decisions, the family's plans, who is in and who is out, and how you handle that knowledge defines you.

The professional shares information generously where sharing serves the work, the chef needs the guest numbers, security needs the movements, the housekeeper needs to know the family returns Thursday, and hoards it only where discretion demands. The politician does the opposite, hoarding information to make himself necessary and doling it out to build obligation, and it is a strategy that works for a while and then collapses, because a house eventually recognises the person who keeps it in the dark to keep himself important, and it routes around him.

Be the person who tells people what they need to do their work, and who is silent only where silence is a duty rather than a manoeuvre.

**13.11 · Agencies and temporary staff**

Very few households run entirely on permanent staff. Agencies place people, cover shortfalls, and supply the extra hands for events, and a large part of your working life will involve people who are in the house for a week, a night, or a season rather than for years.

Handling temporary and agency staff well is its own small discipline, and doing it badly is both a service failure and a security exposure.

Understand first that a temporary member of staff carries none of the house's accumulated knowledge and all of the house's accumulated risk. They do not know the standard, the family's preferences, the geography of the residence, or the things that must never be touched or discussed, and they walk out at the end with everything they saw.

Brief them properly and briefly, on what they need to do the job and on the absolute lines, discretion, no photographs, no conversation about the family, areas that are off limits, and never assume that because they were sent by a reputable agency they arrive knowing your house. They do not. No one does.

Treat agency and temporary staff with exactly the courtesy you extend the permanent team, both because it is right and because it is prudent: the casual waiter poorly treated at a private dinner is the casual waiter who sells a story, and the agency that placed a well-treated temp is the agency that sends you their best people next time. Remember too that these people talk to their agencies, and their agencies talk to the whole profession, so your conduct toward the most junior temporary hand is quietly building or eroding the reputation this chapter closes on.

Nothing you do in a house stays as private as it feels, least of all how you treat the people with the least power in it.

**13.12 · A reputation that travels**

Understand, finally and permanently, the fact that governs every relationship in this chapter: private service is a very small world, and it talks. The senior people who run great houses know one another, move between the same families, use the same handful of agencies, and check quietly with one another before they hire.

Your reputation, good or bad, will arrive at your next post before you do, carried by people you may not even remember, and it will open doors or close them long after you have forgotten the conduct that formed it.

This is the deep reason that every piece of advice in this chapter is also self-interest correctly understood. The colleague you humiliated, the peer whose work you claimed, the junior you treated as furniture, the agency temp you were sharp with, the gossip you traded, none of these stays inside the walls of the house where it happened.

It travels, in a quiet word between two estate managers, in an agency's private note on a candidate, in the memory of a housekeeper who moves to a grander family and is asked, one day, whether she has ever worked with you. The reference that is never written down, the verbal reference, the one professional gives another off the record, is the currency this whole profession actually runs on, and you are building yours in every interaction, whether you attend to it or not.

So build it deliberately. Be the person others want to work with again: reliable, discreet, fair, generous with credit and sparing with blame, calm in a crisis, and incapable of the small cruelties that the powerless remember longest. Treat the newest housemaid and the head of security with the same fundamental respect, because you never know which of them will one day be asked about you, and because the professional who is decent only upward is seen through instantly by everyone standing to the side.

A reputation for competence gets you the interview. A reputation for character, carried by the people you worked beside, is what actually moves you up through the small, watchful, interconnected world you have chosen to enter. Guard it as your single most valuable possession, because within a few years, in this profession, it is exactly that.

**CHAPTER SUMMARY**

A household runs on a dozen relationships beyond the family, and you will accomplish nothing without the cooperation of the housekeepers, chefs, drivers, security, nannies, gardeners, assistants, and estate staff who each hold a domain and guard it. You sit as the hinge between the office above and the house below, with peers to the side, and each direction demands a different manner: usefulness and restraint upward, willing cooperation and scrupulous fairness downward, reciprocity and influence-without-authority sideways. Correct the error and protect the person, always privately and specifically. Read the politics, the favourite, the gatekeeper, the long-tenured resister, the standing war between office and household, and align with no faction. Stay out of the gossip that will mark you, cover for people but never for facts the family needs, and treat turf and information as the currencies they are. Brief temporary staff properly and treat them well. And remember, in every interaction, that the profession is small, that it talks, and that the reputation you build among the people you work beside is the thing that finally carries your career.

## The year

*The calendar these families live by, and how to live inside it*

**LEARNING OBJECTIVES**

Reproduce the seasonal calendar of the UHNW world from memory, month by month, and place any given household on it within your first week. Time your applications to the hiring seasons rather than to your own impatience. Understand migration between residences as the central logistical fact of the year, and know the advance work each move demands. Distinguish the staff who travel from the staff who stay, and know which you are. Prepare a surge period as a campaign, and use a quiet period as the working season it truly is. Read how children's terms, travel, and the financial year each impose their own rhythm on top of the seasonal one. And, hardest of all, learn to protect your own rest in a role that has no natural off-switch, because the year will not protect it for you.

Nobody teaches this, and everyone senior simply knows it. These families move on a calendar, and the calendar is remarkably stable from one year to the next. A house manager who does not know it is permanently a step behind: reacting to a move that was always coming, scrambling for a fixture that sold out months ago, discovering in September that the works should have been booked in June.

Learn the year and you cease to react. You anticipate. You open the chalet before you are asked, you secure the season's tickets before they are gone, you move the wardrobe and the cellar to where the family will be a month before they arrive.

That single habit, anticipation built on a known calendar, is the difference between a house that runs and a house that scrambles, and it is visible to a principal from across a room.

**14.1 · Why the year has a shape at all**

A family of ordinary means lives where it lives and takes a holiday. A UHNW family does the opposite: it does not have a home and some trips, it has a circuit, and the circuit is the home. The residences are not a main house and some others; they are stations on a route the family follows through the year, and the route is set by three forces that rarely change.

The first is weather: wealth moves toward good climate and away from bad, chasing sun in winter and fleeing heat in summer, and the great seasonal migrations of this world are, at bottom, a flight from discomfort that ordinary people simply endure. The second is the social and sporting calendar, a fixed sequence of events, races, tournaments, fairs, galas, regattas, that the family attends partly for pleasure and partly because attendance is how a certain kind of person maintains a certain kind of standing.

The third, and the most rigid of all where it applies, is the school year, which pins the whole family to a place for its duration and releases it, all at once, into travel the moment term ends.

Understand these three forces and the calendar stops being a list to memorise and becomes something you can reason about. When you meet a new house, you do not need to be told its rhythm; you can largely deduce it. Ask where the children are at school and you have found the anchor of the year.

Ask which sport or scene the principal follows and you have found the fixtures that cannot move. Ask where they go to escape the summer and the winter and you have found the two great migrations. The particular families bend all of this, and some ignore it entirely, but the shape is real, and reading it quickly is one of the first marks of a professional who has done this before.

**14.2 · The calendar, season by season**

What follows is the Northern Hemisphere calendar of a Euro-American family, the most common pattern you will meet and the one worth carrying in your head as a default. Gulf, Asian, and Southern Hemisphere families run their own variants, noted where they matter, but the logic of migration and advance work is identical whichever way the seasons fall.

**Period.** Where the world is, and what it asks of you

**December to March, the snow.** The mountains. Aspen, Vail, Jackson Hole, Park City, and Deer Valley in the United States; Gstaad, St Moritz, Courchevel, Verbier, and Zermatt for those who cross to the Alps. Chalets are opened, stocked, and warmed ahead of the family; the best weeks are booked a year out; ski passes, instructors, and mountain restaurants are arranged before arrival. This is a full residence run in a cold and remote place, not a holiday, and the logistics of getting a family, its guests, and its wardrobe up a mountain in winter are considerable.

**Late December, the gathering, then the sun.** Christmas and the new year are very often gathered first at a principal residence, the one fixed familial moment of the year, and then dispersed: the Alps again for some, and for others the winter Caribbean, St Barths, Mustique, the Turks and Caicos, or further, the Maldives and the Seychelles. The turn of the year is simultaneously the most emotionally loaded date in the household and one of the most logistically demanding, and it cannot be improvised.

**January to March, the winter season proper.** Palm Beach opens and fills; the art and auction calendar begins; the ski houses run at full tilt. In the Gulf and much of Asia this is the pleasant season, and households there are at home and busy, entertaining, before the heat returns.

**April, the shoulder.** Easter travel, the first openings of the summer houses, and, for the Gulf families, the beginning of the plan to escape the coming heat. A transitional month, quieter on the surface and busy underneath, because the summer is being prepared while the winter is being closed.

**May to July, the social and sporting season.** The dense, social heart of the European year, and the most diary-intensive stretch you will manage. The Monaco Grand Prix and the Cannes festival in May; the Chelsea Flower Show, Royal Ascot, the Monaco and Mediterranean regattas, Wimbledon, the Henley regatta, and Glastonbury for some, through June and into July; the summer galas and charity balls throughout. Diaries in these weeks become a battle plan of overlapping fixtures, hospitality, wardrobe, and movement, often across several countries in a fortnight.

**July and August, the water.** The Mediterranean at its peak: Saint-Tropez, Antibes, Sardinia's Costa Smeralda, the Balearics, the Greek islands, and the yachts that move between them. In the United States, the Hamptons, Nantucket, Martha's Vineyard, Maine, the lakes, and the Montana and Wyoming ranches. The principal is at play, and the logistics behind the play are relentless: this is peak demand, peak improvisation, and the season in which reputations are made and lost.

**September, the return.** Back to the city, back to school, the working rhythm resumes, the summer houses are closed and deep-cleaned, and the projects saved for the empty months begin in earnest. A hard pivot from leisure to order, and one of the busiest weeks of the year for the staff who manage it.

**October to November, the cultural and philanthropic season.** The great art fairs, Frieze and the autumn auctions; the philanthropic season and its galas; Thanksgiving in American houses, which is a full domestic surge of its own. Winter staff are hired now, and Christmas planning begins in November because Christmas, again, cannot be improvised.

**TWO PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES**

The first is about hiring, and it decides whether you find work this year or next. Seasonal roles, the most realistic first rung for a newcomer, are filled three to four months in advance. Winter chalet staff are recruited in September and October, and again, in a smaller panic, in late November. Summer teams are hired in April and May. If you apply in December for a winter season you are applying, without knowing it, for next winter, and you will conclude the market is closed when in truth you simply arrived after the doors shut. Apply into the hiring season, not into your own impatience.

The second is about work, and it corrects the commonest misconception a newcomer holds. Moves, renovations, deep cleans, and installations are scheduled into the weeks the family is away. The empty house is not your quiet period.

It is your busiest, because it is the only window in which the disruptive, heavy, house-altering work can be done without the family present. The family's absence is your working season, and the real, visible proof of your competence is delivered in the weeks they are not there to watch it being done.

**14.3 · Migration, and the advance work each move requires**

Migration is the single fact from which most of your working year is built. A UHNW family does not simply travel; it relocates its life, repeatedly, and each relocation is a project with a critical path. The amateur thinks of a move as booking the transport.

The professional thinks of it as opening a house at one end while closing another, with the family, its guests, its wardrobe, its documents, and often its vehicles all in motion between the two, and nothing arriving late and nothing left behind.

Learn to run every move against a standing sequence, adjusted to the house but never skipped. Roughly a month out, you confirm the dates, the guest list, and the shape of the stay, and you brief the destination: the house is aired, checked, and brought up to temperature; the systems are tested; the pantry and cellar are stocked to the family's known preferences; the local staff are alerted and rostered; the standing suppliers, florist, laundry, grocer, are put on notice of the dates.

Two weeks out, you handle the personal logistics: travel and transfers booked, any private aircraft or yacht confirmed and provisioned, travel documents and visas checked against the itinerary, medications and prescriptions arranged to cross borders, and the wardrobe planned against the diary of the stay so that what is needed is where it needs to be. The week of the move, you confirm everything twice, you send an arrival brief to the receiving house, and you make sure the departing residence will be closed properly behind the family: perishables cleared, systems set to away mode, security informed, and a deep clean scheduled into the vacancy you have just created.

Two disciplines make the difference between a move that is felt and a move that is invisible. The first is the arrival brief: a short, standing document that tells the receiving house exactly who is coming, when, in what number, with what preferences and dietary needs, so that the family walks into a house that already knows them rather than one learning them at the door.

The second is redundancy of the essential: the passports, the medications, the chargers, the one irreplaceable object the principal always needs, tracked personally and never entrusted to the general baggage. A family will forgive a great deal, but a missing passport at a private terminal is the kind of failure that ends a tenure, and it is entirely preventable by a person who has built the habit of checking the few things that genuinely cannot be replaced on arrival.

Keep, for every residence, a written opening-and-closing protocol, so that the sequence does not live only in your head. Which systems to wake and in what order, which suppliers to call, how long the house needs to reach readiness, where the perishables are cleared to, how the property is secured when empty.

A serious household holds these as documents that anyone competent can execute. The house that keeps them in one person's memory is a house that scrambles the moment that person is ill, on leave, or gone.

**14.4 · The staff who follow, and the staff who stay**

Every migrating household divides its people, whether or not it says so aloud, into those who travel with the family and those who hold a residence in the family's absence, and knowing which you are, in any given post, is fundamental to understanding the shape of your year. The travelling staff, the ones who follow, live the family's calendar directly: they move when the family moves, they work hardest when the family is present, and their year is a series of relocations punctuated by the family's own rhythm of activity and rest.

The house is never fully theirs; wherever the family is, that is where they are. The resident staff, the ones who stay, live the inverse calendar: they are quietest when the family is present in a different residence and busiest when the family is away, because absence is precisely when the deep work, the maintenance, and the projects are done, and it is also when the house is prepared for the next return.

The house manager or estate manager frequently sits across both patterns at once, and this is the peculiarity of the senior role. You may travel with the family for the great migrations and yet remain responsible, from a distance, for the residences they are not in, directing the resident teams by phone and message while managing the household physically around you.

It is why the senior person in a multi-residence house is never truly off the calendar of any one house; you are always, to some degree, running the empty ones as well as the full one. Establish early, in any post, which pattern is yours, because it determines everything about your own year: whether you should expect to live out of a suitcase for months, or to hold one house through the long quiet stretches, or, hardest of all, to do both at once.

There is also a fluid layer worth understanding: the staff engaged only for a season or a surge. Winter chalet teams, summer yacht crew, extra hands hired for a large party or a long stay, sourced through agencies against the calendar and released when the season ends.

As you become senior, hiring, briefing, and managing this seasonal layer becomes part of your year in its own right, and it runs on the same three-to-four-month lead time that governs your own applications. The house that waits until June to find its summer staff is bidding for what is left after the good people are already placed.

**14.5 · The surges, and how to prepare for them**

Certain moments in the year concentrate the household's work into a peak, and these surges, the large party, the wedding, the family gathering at Christmas or a religious festival, the milestone birthday, the long stay with many guests, are where a house is truly tested. They share a structure, and once you can see the structure you can prepare any of them as a campaign rather than survive them as an emergency.

Every surge has the same anatomy. There is a lead time, and the rule is simple: the larger the event, the longer the runway, from weeks for a substantial dinner to the better part of a year for a wedding of any scale. There is a guest dimension, which drives almost everything downstream: the numbers, the accommodation, the dietary and access needs, the transfers, the security clearances.

There is a supplier layer, the caterers, florists, marquee and furniture hire, entertainment, additional cleaners and servers, each of whom must be booked early, briefed precisely, and managed on the day. There is the day itself, which is pure execution against a run-sheet built over the preceding weeks.

And there is the aftermath, the clearing, the returns, the settling of accounts, and the reset of the house, which the amateur forgets to plan for and the professional has scheduled before the first guest arrives.

Prepare a surge by working backwards from the date. Build a critical path: identify the long-lead items, the ones that sell out or book up, and secure those first, before anything else. Hold a single master document, guests, timings, suppliers, budget, responsibilities, that is the one source of truth everyone works from, so that no two people are working from different numbers.

Brief every supplier and every extra hand in writing, against a clear run-sheet, so that on the day people execute rather than ask. Build in contingency deliberately: the weather plan for the outdoor event, the spare capacity, the named person who handles the problem that will arise so that you are free to hold the whole.

And plan the recovery as carefully as the event, because a surge does not end when the guests leave; it ends when the house is reset, the accounts are closed, and the team has been allowed to recover.

The recurring surges are, at least, predictable, and predictability is a gift you should exploit. Christmas, Thanksgiving, the annual summer gathering, the religious festivals the family observes, Ramadan and the Eids in a Muslim household, the High Holy Days in a Jewish one, Diwali, Lunar New Year, each arrives on a known date every year.

Keep a file from one year to the next: what was ordered, from whom, what worked, what failed, what the numbers were. The professional who can open last year's Christmas file in October and begin from a known baseline is worth a great deal more than the one who starts from nothing each December, and the file is the single most useful document you will build in your first year in any house.

**14.6 · The quiet periods, and the work that belongs in them**

The quiet period is the most misunderstood stretch of the year, and the misunderstanding is expensive. When the family is away and the surge has passed, the untrained mind reads the calm as time off. It is not.

The absence of the family is the presence of a working window, and the household's real internal work, the work that cannot be done while the family is in residence, is precisely what belongs here.

Five kinds of work fill a genuine quiet period, and a good house manager has them planned before the vacancy begins. The first is maintenance and deep cleaning: the heavy, disruptive work that a family's presence forbids, the deep clean of a kitchen taken out of use, the servicing of systems, the seasonal check of everything that a house needs and cannot receive while occupied.

The second is projects: the renovation, the redecoration, the installation, the garden works, everything scheduled deliberately into the empty weeks so that the family returns to an improvement rather than an inconvenience. The third is preparation for the next return or the next surge: the standing task of making sure the house is ready, stocked, and repaired before the family or the season arrives.

The fourth is training and development, for the team and for yourself: the quiet weeks are when a team can be properly trained, when new systems can be introduced, when the manuals and protocols can be written or improved, and when you yourself can learn the parts of the craft the busy weeks never allow. The fifth is leave, and it is not an afterthought; it is a planned use of the window, both yours and the team's, because a quiet period spent entirely on projects, with no rest taken, simply moves your exhaustion into the next surge.

Plan the quiet period as deliberately as you plan a surge. Keep a standing list of the deferred work, the things you noticed during the busy weeks and could not act on, the repair you postponed, the system you meant to improve, the supplier you meant to review, so that when the window opens you are not wondering what to do with it.

The professional treats the empty house as the season in which the household is actually improved, and returns it to the family measurably better than they left it. The amateur treats it as a holiday, does the minimum, and is quietly found out when the standard slips.

**14.7 · How children drive the whole calendar**

Where there are children, the school calendar is not one factor among several; it is the master clock, and it governs the family's year more absolutely than the parents' own preferences do. The term dates fix the family in place for their duration, and the moment term ends the family is released, all at once and on a date known a year in advance, into the travel and the migrations described above.

Half-terms and exeats punctuate the term with short, intense bursts of travel. The long summer holiday opens the great Mediterranean and ranch season. The Christmas and Easter holidays anchor the winter and spring migrations.

If you want to predict a family's year, find out where the children are at school and when the terms run, and you will have found the skeleton on which everything else hangs.

The practical loads that come with children are their own recurring surges, and you should know them before they arrive. There is the start of the school year, a genuine logistical peak: uniforms, kit, supplies, transport arrangements, the medical and administrative forms, the settling of a term's rhythm.

There is boarding, where it applies, with its drop-offs and collections, its exeat weekends, its sports fixtures and concerts and parents' events, each a fixed date the family will want to attend and each requiring travel and diary management. There is the rhythm of a term itself, the daily school run, the after-school activities, the tutoring, the sport, which pins the household to a place and a routine for weeks at a stretch.

And there is the transition into and out of every holiday, which is where the school calendar meets the migration calendar and both peak at once.

A particular complication is worth naming, because it catches people out: children of different ages, and children at different schools, often run on different calendars, and a family with several children may be pulled in several directions by term dates that do not align. Managing the overlap, the collection of one child while another is still in term, the holiday that begins for one before it begins for another, is a real and recurring piece of your year, and it rewards a single, shared family calendar that holds every child's dates in one place.

Build that calendar early. It is the document that saves the family from discovering, too late, that the dates it assumed were aligned are not.

**14.8 · The travel-heavy stretches, and the logistics of jet and yacht**

Certain stretches of the year are defined by near-constant movement, the social season, the summer, the run of festivals and fixtures, and in these weeks the logistics of private travel move from an occasional task to the spine of your daily work. You will not usually pilot any of this yourself, but you must understand it well enough to orchestrate it, because the family experiences the seam between one leg and the next as your responsibility, and a good journey is one in which the seams are invisible.

Private aviation runs on its own logic, and the parts that touch you are learnable. A private jet does not depart from a public terminal but from a fixed-base operator, and the door-to-door experience, car to terminal to aircraft, is built to be seamless, which means the ground pieces, the transfers, the timing, the catering loaded aboard, the documents ready, are yours to arrange even when the flight itself is flown by others.

Catering is ordered to the family's known preferences and loaded before departure. Documents, passports and visas, are checked against the itinerary well in advance, because a private flight crosses borders and clears customs like any other, and the informality of the terminal does not extend to the paperwork.

Ground transport waits at both ends. Pets, where they travel, have their own requirements and their own documents. The whole art is in the seams: the family should step from car to cabin and from cabin to car without ever feeling the joins, and the joins are exactly what you have spent the preceding days arranging.

The yacht is a moving residence, and the summer weeks aboard are among the most demanding of the year for the staff who support it. The provisioning is substantial and must be planned around a route that may itself change; the coordination with the captain and crew is constant; the guest movements, the tenders, the transfers ashore, the reservations in port, are yours to arrange from land or aboard; and the itinerary is fluid, weather-dependent, and prone to change at short notice, which means your plans must be built to flex without breaking.

A charter adds a contractual layer, the terms, the deposits, the provisioning arrangements, that you may be asked to manage or oversee. The common thread with the jet is the same: a moving family whose every transition, ship to shore, port to port, must be arranged so that the movement feels effortless to the people inside it and is anything but effortless for the person arranging it.

Two habits protect you across all travel-heavy stretches.
